In the triangle below, what is the length of the shorter leg?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14165760/assets/aeb29243195210194a1f114fdf5146bcbd418180c957d5a1c88c3f1055a5c5c9.png)
current_example.worked_solution:
Let's refer to our standard $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14165760/assets/58993cc083d8561501ea9db70c6d4d886fadc4d4ac3455a1a58de1fe5ceb6e77.png)

Since this is a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle, the length of the longer leg is $\sqrt{3}$ times that of the shorter leg.

Here, the longer leg has length $2,$ and the shorter leg has length $x,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\sqrt{3}x \\ x & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the radical from the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and denominator by the radical:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{2\cdot \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{3}}=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the length of the shorter leg is $\dfrac{2 \sqrt{3}}{3}.$
